turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, that this arrangement leaves me somewhat unsatisfied. One must be careful about such accommodations, especially when one is considering marriage.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I understand, Lady Bracknell. I assure you, my living arrangements are entirely proper and respectable. May I answer any further questions you have, to your satisfaction?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I am not entirely convinced, Mr. Worthing. May I ask about your parents? They must have been prominent figures, surely.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I am afraid, Lady Bracknell, that my parents passed away some years ago. They left me a considerable inheritance, which I have managed with great care and prudence.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I see. The loss of one's parents at a young age can be quite unfortunate. However, it does not explain the peculiarity of your circumstances, Mr. Worthing. Pray, tell me, how did you come to own such a substantial estate?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I inherited the estate from my father, Lady Bracknell. It has been in my family for generations, though I can assure you, the circumstances of my birth are entirely respectable.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must insist, Mr. Worthing, that you provide a clearer account of your origins. The circumstances of one's birth are irrelevant; what matters is one's development since then. But in your case, I find the details somewhat hazy.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I understand your concern, Lady Bracknell. I shall do my best to clarify my background and assure you of my respectability.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I am not entirely convinced by your assurances, Mr. Worthing. The matter of your birth and the subsequent acquisition of your estate remain clouded. It is imperative that you provide a more satisfactory explanation.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I shall endeavor to provide all the information you require, Lady Bracknell. I understand the importance of these matters and wish to reassure you.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I require more than mere assurances, Mr. Worthing. The truth of your background must be unequivocal and beyond reproach. Your reputation, and by extension, Gwendolen's, rests upon this.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I will do my utmost to provide you with the information you seek, Lady Bracknell. My intentions are honorable, and I wish to establish my respectability in every way possible.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I shall be interested to hear your explanation, Mr. Worthing. However, do not waste my time with unnecessary details. Be concise and to the point.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I understand your concerns, Lady Bracknell. I shall provide a clear and concise account of my circumstances.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Let us begin, then. Tell me, Mr. Worthing, how did you come by your fortune?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I encountered a sum of money left by a wealthy gentleman who passed away under mysterious circumstances when I was but a child, Lady Bracknell. This fortune has been the foundation of my current status.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, surely you are not questioning Jack's integrity. He has been honest with you about his past.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I am not questioning Mr. Worthing's integrity, but I must know everything about his background to ensure it is suitable for my daughter.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I appreciate your diligence, Lady Bracknell. May I elaborate further on my circumstances to clarify any doubts you might have?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, it is imperative that all aspects of your background are clear. You must understand, I have the reputation of my daughter to consider.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Gwendolen, the carriage!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: That is satisfactory. What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I dons depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
